title: 147 Assessment of thermal imaging to objectively body condition score mature horses and multiparous gestating beef cows
content:
Abstract
This study explored the opportunity to leverage thermal imaging as an objective means of body condition score (BCS) assessment horses and cattle. The BCS of Quarter Horse (n=98) or Thoroughbred (n=67) breed type horses and mid-gestation beef cows (n=97) were assessed by multiple trained scorers and used to derive and test algorithms to determine BCS based on measurements of surface body temperature obtained from thermal imaging. Animals were assigned an overall BCS, along with BCS scores for specific body sites (the neck, shoulder, withers, ribs, loin, and tailhead in horses; and the brisket, shoulder, ribs and spine, and hips and hooks in cows). Thermal images were collected from one (cows) or both (horses) sides of the body and analyzed for surface temperature in each of the five (cows) or seven (horses) body areas scored. These surface temperature measures were used as features in a random forest regression along with covariates including breed, ambient temperature, cloud coverage (%), housing conditions, blanketing status, individual scorer, and scorer’s location. To facilitate model derivation and testing, each species-specific dataset was randomly divided into three portions: 15% for hyperparameter tuning, 55% for model-training, and 30% for independent evaluation. Models were created to estimate overall BCS, as well as BCS for each specific site assessed. The root mean squared error (RMSE, % mean) was the primary fit statistic used to evaluate model performance. Across all body regions, the RMSE values (% mean) ranged from 7.6% to 10.6% for horses and 6.81% to 13.4% for cows. For comparison to the consistency achieved by human scorers, scorer variability was assessed for both datasets by calculating the coefficient of variation (CV) among scorers. The variability among the eight horse scorers ranged from 13% to 14% and from 10.8% to 12.1% for the five cow scorers, varying with location on the body where the score was assigned. Overall, thermal imaging shows promise as an objective tool for BCS determination in both horses and beef cows. However, future application will require broader datasets to more comprehensively account for conflating factors like environment, housing, and management.
